result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.adamic_adar_index()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute Adamic-Adar index for node pairs. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L8755-L8827){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.adamic_adar_index(ebunch=None) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} For each pair of nodes `(u, v)`, computes `Σ(1 / log(|N(w)|))` for all common neighbors `w`. This gives more weight to common neighbors that themselves have fewer connections (rarer connections are more significant). ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ebunch]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[tuple[Union[int, str], Union[int, str]]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : List of node pairs to compute predictions for. Each pair can use node IDs (integers) or labels (strings). If `None`, computes for all pairs of nodes that are not already connected. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[tuple[int, int, float]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of `(u, v, index)` tuples where index is the Adamic-Adar score. Results are returned with node IDs. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The Adamic-Adar index refines common-neighbor counting by weighting each shared neighbor $w$ by $\dfrac{1}{\log |N(w)|}$: $\mathrm{AA}(u, v) = \sum_{w \in N(u) \cap N(v)} \dfrac{1}{\log |N(w)|}$. The intuition, borrowed from information theory, is that rare neighbors carry more evidence of a real connection than popular hubs everyone touches. The score is unbounded above and empirically beats plain common-neighbor counting on many real networks. Runs in $O(k)$ per pair. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Nodes 2 and 3 share the hub as their only common neighbor, but since the hub has high degree, its contribution is downweighted -- the score stays well below what plain common-neighbor counting would suggest: ::: {#82c9a19f .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph(directed=False) # Create a network with a hub (node 1) and peripheral nodes graph.add_node() # Hub node 1 for i in range(2, 10): graph.add_node() graph.add_edge(1, i) # Hub connected to all graph.adamic_adar_index([(2, 3)]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [(2, 3, 0.48089834696298783)] ``` ::: ::: Comparing directly against `common_neighbors()` on the same pairs makes the downweighting effect clear -- a shared hub counts as 1 common neighbor, but contributes less than 1 to the Adamic-Adar score: ::: {#55f187b1 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph(directed=False) graph.add_cycle_graph(6) pairs = [(1, 3), (1, 4)] list(zip(graph.common_neighbors(pairs), graph.adamic_adar_index(pairs))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [((1, 3, 1), (1, 3, 1.4426950408889634)), ((1, 4, 0), (1, 4, 0.0))] ``` ::: :::
